newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: YACHTING-RACE FAVOURITES RECALLED AFTER FALSE START.
newsitem.headline: YACHTING-RACE FAVOURITES RECALLED AFTER FALSE START.

text.p: The Australian yacht Sydney led the fleet in the 52nd Sydney-to-Hobart race shortly after an extraordinary start on Thursday which saw most of the pre-race favourites restart after prematurely breaking the line.

Hong Kong yacht Exile had led the 95-yacht fleet down Sydney Harbour but was recalled by race officials and suffered a 20-minute penalty after being among a group of yachts which broke the line ahead of the official starter's gun.

The crews aboard other yachts, including German maxi Morning Glory and Australian maxis Brindabella and Amazon, immediately realised their mistakes and rounded the fleet to start again in light northerly winds without incurring a 20-minute penalty.

Exile, a pocket maxi owned by expatriate Australian businessman Warwick Miller, had continued down the harbour after its false start, with Miller and his crew unaware of their breach until called back by race organisers. Yachts recalled by race officials suffer a mandatory 20-minute penalty.
Miller and his crew suffered badly for their mistake. Exile lay becalmed off Sydney Heads in light winds as it tried to sail back down the harbour to start again.

Sydney, a 60-foot yacht designed and helmed by Australian America's Cup veteran Iain Murray, surprised its more fancied rivals by reaching the heads first ahead of Australian maxi Condor, winner of the race in 1983.
Brindabella, owned by Australian businessman George Snow, was runner-up the past two years but made up good time after its restart to pass Condor soon after it left the harbour.

Morning Glory also made good ground after its crew had worked frantically over the past two days to install a new mast in place of the A$380,000 (US$304,000) spar which snapped during a training race last Saturday.

The 95-boat fleet faced a tough run after the wind died shortly after they left Sydney Harbour. A southerly change was expected on Thursday afternoon and there appeared little hope that any would challenge the 21-year-old race record, one of the most prized in international yachting.

In 1975, U.S. maxi Kialoa set a race record of two days 14 hours 36 minutes and 56 seconds after flying down the east coast powered by strong northeasters during most of the 630-nautical mile blue-water classic to Australia's southern island of Tasmania.
